messages.subject: Survival model has a nearly singular matrix and INLA crashes
messages.subject_clean: Survival model has a nearly singular matrix and INLA crashes
messages.body_plain:
I am estimating a large multilevel, recurrent-event, survival model. I am going to overload you with information incase it is relevant, but in short:

Currently, R-INLA is quitting because the matrix is nearly singular,

"Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it..."

For more details:

Every individual within the dataset regularly shops at a store. At some point they were exposed to my treatment. In total, there are about 2 million people, with approximately 150 million shopping trips (pre and post treatment). I am trying to measure the treatment's effect on their shopping pattern.

I've begun with a small sample of 700 hundred shoppers (~50,000 trips). I have encoded the data as one row per shopping trip. There is a time-varying, binary flag that indicates when a shopper was exposed to the treatment (0 before exposure, 1 after exposure).

For the first draft of the model, there is a population level treatment effect and each shopper has an individual-level intercept. The model uses the coxph family. Eventually, I want to include a bunch of customer level features and store level features, but that is after I get this first model to work.

This what the code looks like:

formula = inla.surv(time, status) ~ treatment + f(id, model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list(param=c(1, 1))))

mod = inla(formula, family="coxph", data=df, control.hazard = list(scale.model = TRUE), num.threads = 72, blas.num.threads = 72, control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge"), verbose =  TRUE)

On Fri, 2018-11-02 at 09:29 +0300, endale alemayehu wrote:
> After I fitted the model with INLA, I checked the model fit with CPO
> and PIT. However, the graph of those methods was not seems uniform
> distribution. Thus, this is kindly to ask you on how to improve to
> have uniform distribution of those techniques. Thank you very much.
>

The cpo graph should not be uniform, but PIT we aim for some
uniformity. This is about the difference between the observations and
the predictive distributions (without that data point). For discrete
responses, then these plots are just 'suggestive', like for Poisson
with few counts, I would not trust them to much, while I would for
Poisson with high counts.

There is no generic approach to improve the PIT histogram, beyond
trying to improved the model. I would not be to obsessed by it, though.
The important thing, is that the PIT histogram is not to bad.

H

messages.body_plain:
the issue about 'factors' is that in the freq viewpoint, the common
approach is to chose a reference category, and then everything else is
relative to that one, this is what happen with 'lm()' and relatives,

> model.matrix(~1+x, data=data.frame(x=as.factor(c(1,2,3))))
  (Intercept) x2 x3
1           1  0  0
2           1  1  0
3           1  0  1
attr(,"assign")
[1] 0 1 1
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$x
[1] "contr.treatment"

from a Bayesian point of view, this leads to a non-exchangable prior
for 'x', as the marginal variance depends on the choice of reference
category. As an alternative, you can use the iid which sums to zero,

f(x, model="iid", constr=T)

so that the average effect of 'x' is zero.

this one, explains a third strategy

http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-How-does-inla-deal-with-NA-s-in-the-data-argument-

by setting the expand.factor.strategy="inla", then you'll get a
'singular' expandsion without the reference group, but then only
contrasts are likelihood identifiable. see the refence for details.

there is no single best solution here...

Best
H

I am dealing with a two-level hierarchical model. There are two states, and in each state there are 3 cities. I want to test the effect of variable x on the response variable y, but the effect of x will follow the two hierarchies - city/state. The two state share the same hyperparamters, and the 3 cities in each state share the same hyperparameters.

I didn’t find a way to set two-level hierarchy with INLA. So I defined a new index for each specific city (from 1 to 6), and then the model formula became:

formula = y ~  f(x, model="iid", replicate = new_index)

But in this way, these 6 cities are totally independent but share the same hyperparameters, is it correct?

If correct, it is not exactly what I want. Do you know how to deal with this question?

Thanks,
Ruby

You have an confounding effect here with the Gaussian likelihood, since
basically you have like

y_i = \mu + u_i + \epsilon_i

where both u and epsilon are iid Gaussians. So it might happend, due to
paralellism, that the models estimate that most of the variance is
explained by u and less by epsilon, OR, most of the variance by epsilon
and less by u.

You can control this by the prior for u and epsilon, but its a little
``unusual'' setup unless you know well the variance for one of the
effect.

In terms of waic/dic the differences can you huge, for the different
modes.

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA enthusiasts,

I have a spatial regression model, where two explanatory variables have a spatial effect as provided by the formula below. For those two variables (X3, X4) I would like to calculate the probability that the spatial coefficient is below the mean.  I am stuck on how to make an appropriate lincomb dataframe for the two variables. I have tried to do:

# Reg is spatial polygons dataframe where each line is an administrative unit and Y is my dependent variable and X1, X2, X3, X4 are my explanatory variables. id1 and id2 are the ids of my polygons (e.g. postal codes).

N = length(Reg$Y)
J = length(Reg$id1)

dat.inla.extra <- list(N = N,J = J)

##Linear combinations dataframe - I have only found an approach in a paper, where the author made a lincomb dataframe for one variable (I need this for two variables (X3, X4)

lcs <- inla.make.lincombs(X3= rep(1, dat.inla.extra$J),
                          id1 = diag(dat.inla.extra$J))

form1 = Y~  1 +  X1 + X2 +
  f(id1, X3, model =  "besag", graph= "graph") +
  f(id2, X4, model =  "besag", graph= "graph")

result = inla(form1,family="poisson", data=Reg@data, lincomb = lcs, E=E, control.inla= list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"), control.compute = list(dic=T), verbose = TRUE)

However, this does not seem to work and INLA crashes when I run the model. I have three questions:

1. How should I define the lincomb dataframe?

2. How can I make the lincomb dataframe for two explanatory variables at once?

3. How can I extract the marginals and compute for both variables that the coefficients are below the mean?

Many thanks in advance!

Boris

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running a large number of INLA models, and have a large proportion that are not converging, which I want to look at in more detail. I have several general questions.

1. Is there any way to distinguish models that have converged from ones that have not, from the fit object after the models have run (the ‘large bru’ produced by the lgcp function)?

2. Is there a way to extract the convergence history from a fit object, i.e. the number of iterations run before convergence, and/or the maximum deviation from previous at each iteration? I know these are output to the console during the lgcp function, but I need to extract them afterwards if possible.

3. Is it possible to change the convergence criterion, i.e. from 1% max deviation from previous, to 2%?

Any advice on any of the queries would be much appreciated.

Many thanks in advance,

Charles

}

inla.doc("bym2") give details.

the model 'bym2' defines both the structured and unstructed term, with
sensisble scaling and corrections for disconnected regions in the
graph.

hence,

formulac<-y~ 1 + f(region.struct1,model="bym2",graph="KEN.adj")

is often sufficient, unless you want to change the priors; see the
documentation.

the PC-priors are default for this model, both for the precision and
for the mixing parameter (which prior is computed at run-time,as it
depends on the graph).

Best
H

messages.subject: inla.posterior.sample for an rw2 process
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to estimate predictions that follow an rw2 process. I understand I can predict the data by simply adding the prediction locations/covariates to the input data with an NA for the dependent variable. However, I would like to learn how to use the inla.posterior.sample().

I did search through the list but did not really see a clear example for rw2. If someone would point me in the right direction that would be great. Otherwise, here is, for simplicity, the example from the rw2 documentation:

n = 100
z = seq(0, 6, length.out = n)
y = sin(z) + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
data = data.frame(y = y, z = z)
formula = y ~ f(z, model="rw2")
fit = inla(formula,
  data=data,
  family="gaussian",
  control.compute=list(config=TRUE)
)
ps = inla.posterior.sample(n=100, fit)  # sample from the joint distribution

So I guess my question boils down to, in this case, what is the relationship between the structure matrix ("R") or "Q" (of formulae 1 & 2 in the rw2 document) and the "z:*" (below). That is, how, I do compute the posterior prediction at some new value of "z"?

Thanks,
Jae

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I want to conduct a spatial-temporal model with "slm" model, but it continues to report an error "Error: all(dim(args.slm$W) == c(slm.n, slm.n)) is not TRUE".

Here are my test scripts with Ohio lung cancer data.

remove(list=ls())
my.dir <- paste(getwd(),"/",sep="")

require(INLA)
inla.setOption(scale.model.default=FALSE)

require(splancs)
require(sp)
require(fields)
require(maptools)
require(lattice)
require(abind)
require(spdep)

###################################################
### Code for Section 7.1
###################################################
# You neeed a folder called "Ohio Lung Cancer" inside your working directory (my.dir)
# with the data downloaded from
# https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/datasets

data <- read.csv(paste(my.dir,"OhioRespMort.csv",sep=""))
ohio <- readShapePoly(paste(my.dir,"tl_2010_39_county00",sep=""))
county1 <- data$county
#Ohio.adj <- paste(my.dir,"Ohio.graph",sep="")
Ohio.adj <- poly2nb(ohio)
Ohio.mat <- nb2mat(Ohio.adj)

e1 <- eigen(Ohio.mat)$values
re.idx1 <- which(abs(Im(e1)) < 1e-6)
rho.max1 <- 1/max(Re(e1[re.idx1]))
rho.min1 <- 1/min(Re(e1[re.idx1]))
rho1 <- mean(c(rho.min1, rho.max1))

mmatrix <- as.matrix(rep(0, nrow(data)))   #zero matrix

## Precision matrix for beta coeffients' prior
betaprec <- .0001
Q.beta = Diagonal(n=ncol(mmatrix), betaprec)

## Priors on the hyperparameters
hyper = list(
  prec = list(
    prior = "loggamma",
    param = c(0.01, 0.01)),
  rho = list(
    initial=0,
    prior = "logitbeta",
    param = c(1,1)))

formula.par <- y ~ 1 +  f(county, model="slm",
                          args.slm=list(
                            rho.min = rho.min1,
                            rho.max = rho.max1,
                            W=Ohio.mat,
                            X=mmatrix,
                            Q.beta=Q.beta),
                          hyper=hyper) +
  f(county1,year,model="iid", constr=TRUE) + year

model.par <- inla(formula.par,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

round(model.par$summary.fixed[,1:5],3)

Do you know how to solve this problem?

I am looking forward to your early reply.

Best,
Xiaojun

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm having an issue with using R-INLA to obtained estimates of linear combinations of counts for Poisson data after the link function has been applied. I have random effects (for groups) but am trying to estimate individual-level averages from a model with random (group) effects. I'm using sampling to estimate the linear combinations after the link function has been applied.

I consistently get upwardly biased results with INLA, while with rstanarm the results are more accurate (though much slower) in this situation. I realize that different priors are being used here, but I am struggling to get INLA to give more accurate estimates. Any help would be appreciated greatly as INLA obviously scales much better than Stan for larger datasets (and I like INLA).

Here's a simplified example:

rm(list=ls())

set.seed(1)
N <- 500
num.grps <- 50
grps <- sample(1:num.grps,N,rep=T)
re <- rnorm(num.grps,sd=1.5)
eta <- -1 + re[grps]
y <- rpois(N,lambda=exp(eta))
dat <- data.frame(y,grps)

f <- y ~ 1 + f(grps)
mod <- inla(f,
            data=dat,
            family="poisson",
            control.predictor=list(link=1),
            control.compute=list(config=TRUE)
            )

get.samp <- function(mod,M=1000) {
    samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod)
    latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
}

samp.preds <- get.samp(mod)[,1:nrow(dat)]
samp <- exp(samp.preds)

vec <- apply(samp,1,mean)
quantile(vec,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

## INLA estimates
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%
## 1.374633 1.266518 1.483474

## "Truth" (individual-level)
## mean(dat$y)
## [1] 1.336

require(rstanarm); options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
mod.stan <- stan_glmer(y ~ 1 + (1|grps),
                       data=dat,
                       family=poisson)
samp.stan <- exp(posterior_linpred(mod.stan))
vec <- apply(samp.stan,1,mean)
quantile(vec,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

## Stan estimates
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%
## 1.336078 1.241095 1.437824

* Priors in Bayesian analysis.
* Visualization of results.
* Bayesian data analysis of highly structured data.
